Même signe : répulsion ; signes opposés: Same sign: repulsion; opposite signs: attraction. Rubbing moves electrons, creating nothing. The word "charge": Franklin.
Les Grecs avaient remarqué que l'ambre f: The Greeks had noticed that rubbed amber attracts twigs. In 1600, in De Magnete, the English physician William Gilbert drew from the Greek elektron, amber, a Latin word for bodies that attract: that is where our "electricity" comes from. In the 18th century Benjamin Franklin named the two kinds of charge positive and negative, and coined the word "charge".
Les charges de même signe se repoussent,: Charges of the same sign repel, opposite charges attract. Rubbing creates nothing: electrons change place. A balloon rubbed on hair takes electrons from it, becomes negative and attracts it. Franklin's choice was arbitrary, and he fixed the conventional direction of current before electrons were discovered: in a wire they actually go the other way.
Boucle fermée obligatoire. Série : tout: A closed loop is required. Series: everything goes out together. Parallel: each branch is independent, like at home.
En série, une seule boucle : retirer une: In series, a single loop: remove one lamp and all the others go out, like old fairy lights. In parallel, each lamp has its own loop: they are independent. That is how a house's sockets are wired. If the current finds an almost resistance-free path, that is a short circuit: the current runs away and heats the wires, hence fuses and circuit breakers that cut off before a fire.
Galvani (1780s): the frogs. Volta (1800): the battery, copper, zinc and salt water. The volt is named after him.
Dans les années 1780, à Bologne, Luigi G: In the 1780s in Bologna, Luigi Galvani saw frogs' legs twitch when touched with two different metals. He took it for an electricity specific to living beings. Alessandro Volta disagreed: for him the electricity came from the contact between the two metals, and the frog was only a detector.
Pour le prouver, Volta empile des disque: To prove it, Volta stacked discs of copper and zinc separated by cardboard soaked in salt water. Connect top and bottom with a wire: a continuous current flows. He described this first true battery in a letter to the Royal Society in London on 20 March 1800. It was later understood that the salt water takes part in the reactions, which Volta overlooked. The volt is named after him.
U = R × I (Ohm, 1827). 9 V sur 3 Ω = 3 A: U = R × I (Ohm, 1827). 9 V across 3 Ω = 3 A. Current is not used up, energy is.
La tension U, en volts, pousse le couran: Voltage U, in volts, pushes the current. Resistance R, in ohms, slows it down. Current I, in amperes, is the resulting flow. Georg Ohm related them in 1827 in Die galvanische Kette: U = R × I. With a 9 V battery on a 3 Ω resistor, I = U ÷ R = 9 V ÷ 3 Ω = 3 A. His work was at first received with little enthusiasm; yet the unit of resistance bears his name.
L'image de l'eau aide : la tension est l: The water picture helps: voltage is the pressure, current the flow, resistance the narrowness of the pipe. A long thin wire resists more than a short thick one. And current does not get used up going through a lamp: the same current comes out, it is energy that is given up. Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series, voltage with a voltmeter connected across the terminals.
Série : R = R₁ + R₂. Dérivation : 1/R =: Series: R = R₁ + R₂. Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ (two 100 Ω = 50 Ω). Kirchhoff's laws, 1845.
En série, le courant traverse les résist: In series, the current goes through the resistors one after the other: they add up, R = R₁ + R₂. The current is the same everywhere, the voltage is shared. In parallel, the current has several paths: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂. For two 100 Ω resistors: 1/R = 1/100 + 1/100 = 2/100, so R = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 Ω. Two paths let twice as much current through.
Ces règles se déduisent de la loi d'Ohm: These rules follow from Ohm's law and the two laws Gustav Kirchhoff published in 1845, while still a student. Junction rule: all the current arriving at a junction leaves it again, nothing is lost. Loop rule: around a loop, the voltages balance out. With these two laws you can work out any circuit, however complicated.
C'est le courant qui tue: It is the current that kills
Le danger, c'est le courant à travers le: The danger is current through the body: 30 mA for the RCD. One wire, no current: the bird survives.
Ce qui blesse, c'est le courant qui trav: What harms is the current passing through the body, more than voltage alone. A few tens of milliamperes are enough to cause serious heart trouble. That is why homes have a 30 mA residual-current device: it compares the current going out and the current coming back, and cuts off within a fraction of a second if some escapes, for example through someone.
Un oiseau posé sur un seul câble haute t: A bird sitting on a single high-voltage line is safe: both its feet are at the same potential, no current passes through it. The danger would come from touching two lines at once, or a line and the pylon. In France the household supply is 230 V AC, 50 Hz; North America uses about 120 V at 60 Hz.
P = U × I : 230 V × 10 A = 2 300 W. Watt: P = U × I: 230 V × 10 A = 2,300 W. Watt = joule per second.
Le watt et le joule ne mesurent pas la m: The watt and the joule do not measure the same thing. The joule is an energy, the watt a power, that is, energy per second: 1 W = 1 J/s. A 5 W bulb spends 5 joules every second. An LED gives as much light as an incandescent bulb using about 5 to 8 times less, because the old one turned most of the electricity into heat.
E = P × t : 2 kW pendant 3 h = 6 kWh. 1: E = P × t: 2 kW for 3 h = 6 kWh. 1 kWh = 3.6 million joules. Standby costs through its duration.
Sur une facture, on paie une énergie, en: On a bill you pay for energy, in kilowatt-hours: power multiplied by time, E = P × t. A 2,000 W heater, that is 2 kW, on for 3 hours uses E = 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kWh. A 5 W bulb on for 1,000 hours: E = 5 W × 1,000 h = 5,000 Wh = 5 kWh. One kilowatt-hour is 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 joules.
Le piège : un appareil en veille consomm: The trap: an appliance on standby uses little per hour, often a few watts, but 24 hours a day. A few watts all year round end up weighing more than a powerful appliance used for a few minutes. To know what costs money, always multiply the power by the time in use.

En 1841, James Prescott Joule mesure la: In 1841 James Prescott Joule measured the heat given off by a wire carrying a current: it is proportional to the resistance and to the square of the current. Combining P = U × I with Ohm's law U = R × I gives P = R × I². That is Joule heating: the toaster, the kettle, the heater and the fuse that melts all use it.
Ce carré explique le transport à très ha: That square explains transmission at very high voltage. For the same power P = U × I, raising the voltage lowers the current. Yet losses in the cables equal R × I²: dividing the current by 10 divides the losses by 10 × 10 = 100. That is why lines leave power stations at hundreds of thousands of volts.
Un courant crée un champ magnétique (Ørs: A current creates a magnetic field (Ørsted, 1820). Electromagnet: Sturgeon, 1824. Motor: electricity → motion.
En 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted remarque: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a wire carrying a current deflects the needle of a nearby compass. Tradition says it happened during a lecture. It is the proof that electricity and magnetism are linked: a current creates a magnetic field around it. André-Marie Ampère worked out the laws within a few weeks; the unit of current bears his name.
Enroulez le fil autour d'un noyau de fer: Wind the wire around an iron core and the field concentrates: that is the electromagnet, invented by William Sturgeon in 1824. Unlike a magnet, it can be switched on and off: scrapyard cranes, doorbells, loudspeakers. In an electric motor, these forces turn a shaft: electrical energy becomes motion.
Un champ qui varie crée un courant (Fara: A changing field creates a current (Faraday, 1831). Alternator = magnet turning past coils.
En 1831, Michael Faraday fait l'inverse: In 1831 Michael Faraday did the reverse: he moved a magnet near a coil of wire, and a current appeared in it. Not when the magnet is still, only when the field changes. That is electromagnetic induction. Faraday, a bookbinder's apprentice who became Humphry Davy's assistant, used little beyond the simplest algebra: he thought in lines of force, an image that would guide Maxwell.
Presque toute notre électricité vient de: Almost all our electricity comes from this. In an alternator, a magnet turns past coils: coal, gas, nuclear, dam or wind turbine only serve to turn it. The motor does the reverse, and some electric cars do both, recovering energy when braking. The induction hob too: its changing field creates currents in the bottom of the pan, which heats by Joule heating.
Earth's field = liquid iron in the core. The Arctic holds a magnetic south pole. Auroras = solar particles guided to the poles.
Ce champ nous protège. Il dévie la plupa: This field protects us. It deflects most of the charged particles coming from the Sun. Near the poles some get in and excite the oxygen and nitrogen of the upper atmosphere, which give off green, red or violet light: those are the polar auroras.
Maxwell (1865) : la lumière est une onde: Maxwell (1865): light is an electromagnetic wave. Hertz (1886): radio waves exist. Marconi (1901): the Atlantic.
En 1865, James Clerk Maxwell met en équa: In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell put electricity and magnetism into equations. His equations predict waves travelling at a speed he calculates: that of light. He concluded that light is itself an electromagnetic wave. A changing electric field creates a magnetic field, which in turn creates an electric field: the wave sustains itself, even in a vacuum.
Restait à le prouver. À partir de 1886,: It still had to be proved. From 1886 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected radio waves in his laboratory. Asked about their applications, he is said to have answered: "Nothing, I guess." Fifteen years later, in 1901, Guglielmo Marconi sent an "S" in Morse across the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland.
Même onde, fréquences différentes. c = λ: Same wave, different frequencies. c = λ × f: Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz = 12.5 cm. Ionising: part of UV, X, gamma.
Plus la fréquence est haute, plus chaque: The higher the frequency, the more energy each grain of light, each photon, carries. Only part of the ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have enough to tear off electrons and damage DNA: they are ionising radiation, hence sunburn. Radio waves and Wi-Fi do not have enough: they can heat, not break DNA.
Röntgen (1895) : rayons X, premier Nobel: Röntgen (1895): X-rays, first Nobel Prize in Physics (1901). Spencer (1945): the microwave, born of a melted chocolate bar.
En 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen découvre des ra: In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen discovered unknown rays, which he called X, able to pass through flesh and reveal bones. In 1901 he received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics, and refused to patent his discovery. About six weeks after the discovery he was already X-raying his wife's hand.
Le radar, développé intensément pendant: Radar, developed intensively during the Second World War, sends out waves and listens for their echo. In 1945 at Raytheon, engineer Percy Spencer was working near a radar magnetron when a chocolate bar melted in his pocket: from this came the microwave oven, which agitates the water molecules in food.
ENIAC : plus de 17 000 tubes. Diode = se: ENIAC: more than 17,000 tubes. Diode = one way. Capacitor = store of charges released at once.
Les premiers ordinateurs calculaient ave: The first computers calculated with vacuum tubes, glass bulbs that let a current of electrons through or block it. ENIAC, completed in 1945 in the United States, had more than 17,000 of them. They got hot, used a lot of power and burned out regularly: finding the dead tube was part of the job.
Tout l'enjeu de l'électronique est là :: That is what electronics is all about: controlling one current with another. The diode, the simplest component, lets current through in one direction only; it is used to turn alternating current into direct current. The capacitor stores charges and releases them in one go, as in a camera flash.
Un interrupteur sans pièce mobile: A switch with no moving parts
Transistor : Bell, 1947, germanium, Nobe: Transistor: Bell, 1947, germanium, Nobel 1956. A small signal controls a large current.
En décembre 1947, aux laboratoires Bell,: In December 1947, at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain got the first transistor working, a small germanium device; William Shockley, their boss, soon designed a more practical version. The three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. Bardeen received a second in 1972, for superconductivity.
Le transistor est fait d'un semi-conduct: The transistor is made of a semiconductor: a material that conducts less well than a metal, but whose conduction can be controlled. A small current or voltage on one terminal controls a large current between the other two. It serves as an amplifier in a radio, and as an ultra-fast switch in a computer. Silicon replaced germanium, hence Silicon Valley.
Circuit intégré : Kilby 1958 (germanium): Integrated circuit: Kilby 1958 (germanium), Noyce 1959 (silicon). Moore's law: doubling every two years.
Le 12 septembre 1958, chez Texas Instrum: On 12 September 1958 at Texas Instruments, Jack Kilby demonstrated the first integrated circuit: several components on a single piece of germanium. About six months later Robert Noyce, at Fairchild, made a silicon version, much easier to manufacture. Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000; Noyce, who died in 1990, could no longer share it.
En 1965, Gordon Moore remarque que le no: In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of transistors per chip was doubling at a steady rate: every year, then, in 1975, he revised it to every two years. This "Moore's law" held for decades. A large 2023 processor has from a few tens to more than a hundred billion transistors. LEDs are diodes too: the blue LED, which made white light possible, won the 2014 Nobel Prize.
Thermique = eau chauffée, vapeur, turbin: Thermal = heated water, steam, turbine, alternator. Plumes = water vapour. Solar: Becquerel, 1839.
Une centrale thermique, au charbon, au g: A thermal power station, coal, gas or nuclear, always does the same thing: heat water. The steam turns a turbine, the turbine drives an alternator, and Faraday's induction does the rest. In a nuclear plant the heat comes from the fission of uranium nuclei. The big white plumes from the cooling towers are not smoke but water vapour.
Les éoliennes et les barrages font tourn: Wind turbines and dams turn the alternator directly, without steam. The solar panel has nothing that turns: it converts light into electricity through the photovoltaic effect, observed by Edmond Becquerel in 1839, at 19. In 2023, according to RTE, nuclear power produced about 65 % of France's electricity.
Edison : continu. Westinghouse et Tesla: Edison: direct current. Westinghouse and Tesla: alternating current. AC won thanks to the transformer.
À la fin du XIXe siècle, Thomas Edison d: At the end of the 19th century Thomas Edison championed direct current; George Westinghouse, who licensed Nikola Tesla's motor patents, championed alternating current. Edison's 110 V DC did not reach beyond about a mile: a small power station was needed for each neighbourhood. In 1882 his lighting company set up in New York on that model.
L'alternatif gagne grâce au transformate: Alternating current won thanks to the transformer, which only works with a varying current, since it relies on induction. It lets you raise the voltage to transmit far with few losses, then lower it again at the user's end. In France the current changes direction a hundred times a second: 50 Hz. The 1892 merger that created General Electric ended the battle.
Production = consommation à chaque insta: Production = consumption at every moment, otherwise the frequency drifts. Storage: pumped storage, batteries (Nobel 2019).
Le réseau a une contrainte que peu de ge: The grid has a constraint few people know: at every moment, production must equal consumption. If more is consumed than produced, the frequency drops below 50 Hz; too large a gap, and outages are triggered to protect the grid. On a winter evening, when everyone gets home and cooks, you need sources that start fast.
Le vent et le soleil ne se commandent pa: Wind and sun cannot be ordered: you have to store or supplement. Pumped-storage stations pump water up into a lake when electricity is plentiful and run it through turbines when it is short. Lithium-ion batteries play the same role on a smaller scale; they earned Goodenough, Whittingham and Yoshino the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 (Leibniz, 1705). 8: 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 (Leibniz, 1705). 8 bits = 256 values. A transistor: on or off.
En binaire, on n'a que deux chiffres, 0: In binary there are only two digits, 0 and 1, and each place is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8… So 1011 = 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 11. Leibniz set out this arithmetic in a memoir published in 1705. With 3 bits you can code 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 values; with an 8-bit byte, 2⁸ = 256.
Pourquoi deux chiffres ? Parce qu'un tra: Why two digits? Because a transistor is very good at two things: letting through or blocking. Text, images, sounds: everything is coded in 0s and 1s. A detail about units: under the International System, a kilobyte is 1,000 bytes; 1,024 bytes is called a kibibyte.
Boole : la logique devient algèbre. Shan: Boole: logic becomes algebra. Shannon (1937): circuits compute it. AND, OR, NOT are enough for everything.
Au XIXe siècle, George Boole fait de la: In the 19th century George Boole turned logic into algebra: true and false become 1 and 0, and "and", "or", "not" become operations. In 1937, aged 21, Claude Shannon showed in his master's thesis at MIT, published in 1938, that relay circuits can carry out all of this algebra. It has been called possibly the most important master's thesis of the century.
La porte ET donne 1 seulement si ses deu: The AND gate gives 1 only if both its inputs are 1; the OR gate gives 1 if at least one is 1; the NOT gate inverts. Built from a few transistors, these gates are assembled into adders, memories, then processors. A computer is, at bottom, just a huge assembly of these three decisions.
Des plans de Babbage au bug de 1947: From Babbage's plans to the 1947 bug
Babbage : la machine jamais construite ;: Babbage: the machine never built; Lovelace (1843): the first program. Von Neumann (1945): program and data together.
Au XIXe siècle, Charles Babbage conçoit: In the 19th century Charles Babbage designed the analytical engine, a programmable mechanical calculator. It was never built in his lifetime. Yet in 1843 Ada Lovelace published its first program: a calculation of the Bernoulli numbers. She also sensed that the machine could handle things other than numbers, music for example.
La guerre accélère tout. En 1943-1944, C: The war sped everything up. In 1943-1944 Colossus helped Bletchley Park break encrypted German messages; it remained secret until the 1970s. In 1945 John von Neumann described the architecture in which program and data share the same memory, that of almost all our computers. And in 1947 Grace Hopper's team taped into their logbook a moth found in a relay: "first actual case of bug being found".
Un courant ne circule que dans une boucl: A current flows only in a closed loop: from the battery, through the wires, through the lamp, and back to the battery. An open switch breaks the loop and the lamp goes out. Metals conduct because some of their electrons are free to move; plastic, glass or rubber hold them back: they are insulators, hence cable sheathing. This difference between conductors and insulators was discovered by the Englishman Stephen Gray in 1729: a thread held up by metal lost its charge, one held up by silk kept it, and he made electricity travel 800 feet, about 240 m.
La puissance électrique P, en watts, est: Electrical power P, in watts, is the product of voltage U and current I: P = U × I. An appliance on 230 V drawing 10 A uses P = 230 V × 10 A = 2,300 W. The other way round, a 2,000 W kettle draws I = P ÷ U = 2,000 ÷ 230 ≈ 8.7 A. The watt is named after James Watt, the steam-engine engineer. His great improvement to Newcomen's engine, the separate condenser, dates from 1769.
L'aiguille d'une boussole s'aligne sur l: A compass needle lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, produced by the motion of liquid iron in the outer core. Classic trap: the needle's north pole is attracted by a magnetic south pole. The pole in the Arctic is therefore, magnetically speaking, a south pole. And breaking a magnet in two does not separate its poles: each piece becomes a complete magnet. That the Earth itself is a magnet was proposed by the Englishman William Gilbert, physician to Elizabeth I, in 1600 in De Magnete, after moving a needle around a small sphere of lodestone, the terrella.
Radio, micro-ondes, infrarouge, visible,: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays: it is the same wave at different frequencies. All travel at the speed of light c, about 300,000 km/s, and satisfy c = λ × f: wavelength times frequency. For Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz: λ = c ÷ f = 300,000,000 m/s ÷ 2,400,000,000 Hz = 0.125 m, that is 12.5 cm. Our eye sees only a thin slice, from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). The two invisible neighbours of that slice were discovered one after the other: infrared in 1800 by William Herschel, with a thermometer placed beyond the red of a prism's spectrum, and ultraviolet in 1801 by Johann Ritter, with silver chloride paper that darkened beyond the violet.
